parole.significato: A member of an aboriginal North American people closely related to the Odawa and Ojibwe, and living mainly in Quebec.
parole.testo: From Canadian French algonquin, from earlier algoumequin, from either Maliseet elakómkwik ("these are our relatives") or Mi'kmaq algoomeaking (“at the place of spearing fish and eels”).

parole.significato: Thong(s) of rawhide or sinew used as cord, lacing, or webbing, in the manufacture of snowshoes, braided straps and tump…
parole.testo: First attested around 1800–10. From Canadian French, from Mi'kmaq ápapíj (“cord, thread”), diminutive of ápapi, from Proto-Algonquian *aʔlapa·py, *aʔlapa·pyi, from *aʔlapy- (“net”) + *-a·py (“string”).

parole.significato: An arid terrain characterized by severe erosion of sedimentary rocks.
parole.testo: From earlier Bad Lands, calque of Canadian French mauvaises terres à traverser (“bad lands to cross”), itself a calque of Lakota Makȟóšiča (from makȟá (“land”) + o- (attributive prefix) + šíča (“bad”)).

parole.significato: Dried buffalo or cow dung, sometimes used as fuel by pioneers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Canadian French bois de vache (literally “cow wood”).

parole.significato: The pronghorn antelope.
parole.testo: From Canadian French [Term?].

parole.significato: female French-Canadian
parole.testo: Borrowed from Canadian French Canadienne.

parole.significato: Any of several North American subspecies Rangifer tarandus of the reindeer.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Canadian French caribou, from Mi'kmaq qalipu (“caribou”; compare qalipi, “to shovel snow”), from Proto-Algonquian *maka·lipowa (“caribou”, literally “it shovels snow”).

parole.significato: A convenience store, especially one that sells alcohol.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Canadian French dépanneur.

parole.significato: A collection of stray ice crystals that form in fast-moving water.
parole.testo: From Canadian French frasil, frazil, fraisil, from French fraisil (“coal cinders”), from Old French faisil.

parole.significato: A form of poutine made with spaghetti sauce instead of gravy.
parole.testo: From Italian + poutine, a calque of Canadian French poutine italienne; from being a variant of poutine that uses an Italian-style tomato-based pasta sauce instead of gravy.

parole.significato: The dialect of working-class Quebecers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Canadian French joual.

parole.significato: A sport played on a field between two opposing teams using sticks (crosses) and a ball, whereby one team defeats the ot…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Canadian French la crosse (“the stick”).

parole.significato: A form of stiff leather made from rawhide.
parole.testo: From Canadian French parflèche, equivalent to French par(er) (“to parry”) + French flèche (“arrow”).

parole.significato: Squashberry, lowbush cranberry (Viburnum edule).
parole.testo: Likely from Canadian French pembina, pimbina, from Cree nîpiminâna or Ojibwe niibiminaa, an earlier form of aniibimin (“high-bush cranberry”).

parole.significato: beaver pelt
parole.testo: From Canadian French, from French poilu (“hairy”). Doublet of poilu.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of the province of Quebec, Canada or the Quebec City, Quebec.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Canadian French Québécois.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to the province of Quebec, Canada or its variety of French.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Canadian French québécois.

parole.significato: Hulled Indian corn, or a stew made of this.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Canadian French sagamité, from an Algonquian language; compare Cree ᑭᓵᑲᒥᑌᐚᐳᕀ (kisaakamitewaapoy, “hot water”).

parole.significato: A roughly-built hut or cabin.
parole.testo: From Canadian French chantier (“lumberjack's headquarters”). An alternative theory that the word derives from Irish seantí (meaning "old house") is not considered likely by lexicologists. * (unlicensed pub): New Zealand from 1848.

parole.significato: A young lumberjack.
parole.testo: From shanty + boy, from Canadian French chantier (“lumberjack's headquarters”).

parole.significato: Any of several North American larches, of the genus Larix.
parole.testo: From Canadian French tamarac, believed to derive from an Algonquian word. In European languages there was contamination between tacamahac, from Nahuatl, and various Algonquian words containing the final Proto-Algonquian *-a·xkw- (“hardwood or deciduous tree”), including the sources of tamarack and h

parole.significato: Lake trout, Salvelinus namaycush, a freshwater char of northern North America.
parole.testo: Via Canadian French from an Algonquian word.

parole.significato: A knitted hat, usually conical but of varying shape, often woollen, and sometimes topped by a pom-pom or tassel.
parole.testo: 1871. Assimilated from Canadian French tuque. Likely to be a hypercorrection from the time that toque was already in the dictionaries when they did not yet list tuque as a kind of hat. parole.significato: A type of traditional French-Canadian meat pie, usually made with pork.
parole.testo: From Canadian French tourtière, from a cooking vessel of the same name, from French tourte (“meat pie”). There is a common false etymology that it derives from the alternative meaning tourte (“passenger pigeon”).

parole.significato: A trader, particularly in furs, who worked (and explored) in the area of Canada and the northern United States from the…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Canadian French voyageur.

parole.significato: A fish from any of several freshwater populations of the Atlantic salmon, Salmo salar.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Canadian French ouananiche, from Montagnais, from wanans ("salmon") + -is (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: A member of this people.
parole.testo: From a phonetic rendering of Canadian French Cris, short for Christinaux, from either Algonquin Kirishtinó, or Cree Kenisteniwuik.

parole.significato: A dish consisting of French fries topped with cheese curds and gravy, eaten primarily in Canada.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Canadian French poutine (“French fries with cheese curds and gravy; any of various kinds of pudding”); further etymology uncertain, possibly either: * a variant of French pouding (“pudding”), borrowed from English pudding (possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew- (“to swell”
